faq.a: Check volume status, start a fluid challenge if hypovolaemic, and reassess output after 30 minutes.
faq.q: What is the first step when a patient has oliguria on the ward?

faq.a: Yes; early AKI may present with oliguria before creatinine rises.
faq.q: Can a patient have normal creatinine but low urine output?

faq.a: Severe malaria can cause acute tubular necrosis; falling output signals renal involvement and need for aggressive fluids.
faq.q: Why is urine output important in malaria?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with severe malaria has urine output 40 mL/h. What immediate management steps would you take? — Assess volume status, give isotonic fluids 20–30 mL/kg, stop nephrotoxic drugs, monitor electrolytes.

How does oliguria help differentiate septic shock from cardiogenic shock? — Both have low output, but septic shock often shows warm extremities and high cardiac output; cardiogenic shock shows pulmonary edema and low cardiac output.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy presents with polyuria and nocturia. What causes should you consider? — Diabetes mellitus (ART‑induced), diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia; check glucose and serum sodium.
Why is a bedside urine output chart more reliable than a single 24‑hour collection in low‑resource settings? — It captures trends, detects rapid changes, and does not require laboratory facilities.
What urinary findings would point toward glomerulonephritis rather than pre‑renal AKI? — Presence of red blood cell casts and protein >1+ on dipstick.

In a child with sickle‑cell disease, urine output drops suddenly. What life‑threatening complication must you rule out? — Acute renal failure from vaso‑occlusive crisis; assess for hemoglobinuria and treat with aggressive hydration.

How would you manage an anuric patient when dialysis is unavailable? — Optimize fluid balance, correct electrolytes medically, treat underlying cause, arrange urgent transfer to a centre with dialysis.
What is the significance of a tea‑coloured urine in a patient with severe malaria? — Indicates hemolysis; monitor for renal pigment nephropathy and consider early renal support.
ai.title: Urine Output Assessment
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Urine output reflects kidney function, fluid balance and hemodynamics. Recognising oliguria, anuria and polyuria guides urgent management and diagnosis of common tropical and low‑resource conditions.

b: Normal adult: 0.5–1 mL/kg/h (≈30–80 mL/h).
Oliguria: <0.5 mL/kg/h.
Anuria: <100 mL/24 h.
Polyuria: >3 L/24 h or >2.5 mL/kg/h.
sections.p: Urine output is the volume of urine excreted per unit time, normally 0.5–1 mL/kg/h in adults. It integrates renal perfusion, glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and systemic fluid status.

b: Fluid loss → decreased output; fluid overload → high output.
Nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides, NSAIDs) reduce GFR.
Sepsis, severe malaria, TB meningitis can cause acute kidney injury (AKI).
Obstructive causes: enlarged prostate, schistosomal bladder disease.
sections.p: Assess urine output quantitatively, note colour, clarity and any sediment. Relate changes to volume status, medications, infections and intrinsic renal disease.

b: Oliguria in septic shock signals need for fluids and vasopressors.
Anuria after severe malaria suggests renal cortical necrosis.
Polyuria with diabetes mellitus or uncontrolled diabetes insipidus needs glucose control.
Dark, tea‑coloured urine may indicate hemolysis (e.g., sickle‑cell crisis).
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, urine output is a bedside marker for shock, AKI and response to therapy when labs are limited.

t.b: Is there protein, blood or glucose? Positive protein suggests glomerular disease; blood may indicate infection or hematuria; glucose points to uncontrolled diabetes.
What is renal function? Rising creatinine confirms AKI; electrolyte derangements guide replacement.
Is there bladder distension or hydronephrosis? Detects obstruction when imaging is scarce.
What cells or casts are present? Casts differentiate tubular vs glomerular injury.

b: Fluid resuscitation: isotonic crystalloids 20–30 mL/kg for hypovolaemia; avoid overload in heart failure.
Avoid nephrotoxins: stop NSAIDs, adjust aminoglycoside dose.
Treat infections promptly: antimalarials for severe malaria, antibiotics for sepsis, anti‑TB drugs for renal TB.
Consider renal replacement therapy if anuria >12 h with refractory hyperkalaemia or fluid overload and no dialysis available → refer to higher centre.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then optimise fluid balance and monitor output every hour in acutely ill patients.

b: Always ask: "How much urine in the last hour?"
Document colour and any sediment.
Correlate output with blood pressure, capillary refill and mental status.
In resource‑limited wards, a bedside chart of hourly output is essential.
sections.p: Focus on quantitative output, trends, and linking to clinical picture.

b: Assuming low output is always due to dehydration – ignore possible AKI.
Neglecting to measure output in patients on diuretics – may mask polyuria.
Relying solely on serum creatinine in early AKI – output changes precede labs.
Ignoring urine colour changes that hint at hemolysis or bilirubin.
sections.p: Misinterpretation of urine output can delay critical care.

whenToSeekHelp: Anuria lasting >6 h with hypotension or altered mental status.
Rapidly rising creatinine (>0.3 mg/dL in 48 h) plus oliguria.
Severe electrolyte disturbance (e.g., K⁺ >6.5 mmol/L) with low output.
